accepted.reason: Good observation–target alignment: hospitalization admissions plausibly lag an infectious proxy, and delayed_I is explicitly recommended. Low complexity and avoids an explicit H compartment, which is likely weakly identifiable with only 31 training weeks and a single high-peaked season. No fractional memory, reducing overfitting risk.

Useful as a minimal baseline to test whether an explicit lag is actually needed; still aligned with recommended delayed_I mapping (with 0-week delay). Low parameterization supports identifiability on short single-season data, though it is less semantically plausible than a short lag for hospitalizations.

Keeps the recommended delayed_I observation and a plausible 1-week lag while adding only one major mechanism (waning). Could help if the tail/persistence cannot be captured by SEIR alone, without introducing an explicit H compartment. However, waning is at risk of weak identifiability in a single season.

rejected.reason: Combines two potentially confounded flexibilities in short single-season data: allowing waning (SEIRS) while also removing the admission lag (0-week delayed_I). This increases identifiability risk (lag vs waning tradeoff) and can overfit late-season levels/tails without clear semantic support for zero lag in hospitalization-rate targets.

suggested_edits.edit: Constrain/regularize waning to be slow relative to the season length (i.e., keep SEIRS close to SEIR) to reduce weak identifiability and spurious oscillation; keep the 1-week delay as specified.
If retained as a baseline, explicitly frame it as a diagnostic for near-zero lag rather than a primary mechanistic choice, since hospitalization-rate targets more commonly lag infections.
